children.text: A UNESCO World Heritage marine park reached by an overnight boat trip of more than
10 hours
from Puerto Princesa. Accessible only by liveaboard from March to
June
each year, it offers world-class diving with sharks and towering coral walls.
Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park sits in the middle of the Sulu Sea, about
150km

southeast of Puerto Princesa. It is made up of the North Atoll, the South Atoll, and the small Jessie Beazley Reef, and the protected area covers roughly 97,000 hectares. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site in
, had its boundaries expanded in
, and is also designated as a Ramsar wetland.

No one lives here permanently. The only dry land is Bird Islet and South Islet, where seabirds nest, and a ranger station built on a sandbar at the southern tip of the North Atoll. Around a dozen rangers from the Philippine Navy, the Coast Guard, and the Cagayancillo municipal government take turns staying on-site to guard against illegal fishing. Decades of strict protection have allowed about 600 fish species, roughly 360 coral species, more than 10 shark species, several kinds of whales and dolphins, and hawksbill and green sea turtles to thrive here.
Tubbataha's defining feature is how hard it is to reach. The Sulu Sea has rough seas for most of the year, so licensed liveaboards operate for only about three months, from
mid-March
to
mid-June
, when the water calms down. Day trips or island stays are not possible — every visit is a multi-night diving trip aboard a boat, five or six nights or more.

Coral walls that plunge hundreds of meters straight down, schools of grey reef, whitetip, and blacktip sharks, thousands of jacks and barracuda, and, if you're lucky, whale sharks and manta rays. It's a bucket-list destination for experienced divers, but strong currents and mostly open-water diving make it better suited to intermediate and advanced divers than beginners.
Drift dives follow terrain where a shallow coral plain suddenly drops away into an endless wall. Giant fan corals and sponges cover the wall, and on days with visibility of
or more, the view is overwhelming.

Well-known spots include "Shark Airport," where whitetip sharks rest on the sandy bottom, and points along the outer wall patrolled by grey reef sharks. Seeing dozens of sharks on a single dive is common.
A small reef about
20km
northwest of the main atolls, known for its especially healthy coral and frequent turtle and large-fish sightings.
The Delsan Wreck on the South Atoll and the Malay Wreck let you see coral-covered hulls surrounded by schools of fish.
The only place visitors can go ashore. You'll get a look at the rangers' living quarters and conservation work, and can buy souvenirs and items that support the park.

As you pass near Bird Islet, you can watch thousands of seabirds — brown boobies, red-footed boobies, sooty terns, and more — fill the sky from the deck of the boat. Only researchers and rangers are permitted to land on the island.

blocks.title: Night diving and life on board

children.text: Life on the boat itself — alternating between three or four dives a day and meals and rest in between — is the heart of the trip. The stars at night and the glow of bioluminescent plankton are gifts you can only experience this far out at sea.

It's about
1 hour 20 minutes

from Manila to Puerto Princesa International Airport (PPS), and there are also direct flights from Cebu. Since most liveaboards depart from Puerto Princesa, it's safest to arrive the day before departure.
Tubbataha can only be reached by a licensed liveaboard. More than a dozen boats are licensed each season, and operators typically include airport/hotel pickup and transfer to the port.
The crossing from Puerto Princesa port to Tubbataha takes about
10–12 hours
overnight. Some operators run longer itineraries connecting to Coron, Cebu, and other ports.
The park cannot be visited by private charter or an ordinary bangka, and entering the park without permission from the Tubbataha Management Office (TMO) is punishable by law.
The park conservation fee is

per person (free for children 12 and under), payable in pesos only, and the operator pays it on your behalf when obtaining the park entry permit. You can see the list of permitted liveaboards and the rules on the
official Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park website
Tricycles are the main form of transport in Puerto Princesa; the ride from the airport to a hotel in town takes about
10–15 minutes
and costs about
per tricycle.
Tubbataha opens around
mid-March
each year and closes by
mid-June
. The exact opening and closing dates are set annually by the park management office, so check the latest notice. From late
March
through
May
, the sea is calmest and visibility is at its best, with water temperatures around 27–29°C, so a 3mm wetsuit is enough.
Early in the season, in
March
, some swell may still linger, and conditions grow more unsettled closer to
June
as the southwest monsoon approaches. On the plus side, whale shark and manta ray sightings are often reported in
June
. Because the season is short and the number of boats limited, the popular
April–May
departures often sell out 9 to 12 months in advance.

During the Tubbataha trip, all meals and lodging are on the boat. Liveaboards typically offer twin or quad cabins, most with air conditioning and either private or shared bathrooms. Three meals a day plus snacks between dives are included, usually served buffet-style with a mix of Filipino and Western dishes. Let the operator know in advance about any allergies or dietary restrictions when booking.
Before and after the trip, you'll stay in Puerto Princesa. There are plenty of mid-range hotels around Rizal Avenue and near the airport for about

a night. After disembarking, it's a good way to wrap up the trip with a meal at a long-running seafood restaurant like Puerto Princesa's famous Ka Lui, or a bowl of chao long, the noodle soup brought by Vietnamese immigrants.

In practice you'll need at least an Advanced Open Water certification, and some operators require a minimum number of logged dives (often 30–50 or more). It's worth brushing up on drift diving and SMB use beforehand.
A surface marker buoy (SMB), dive computer, and whistle are essential personal gear. Some operators recommend a personal locator beacon (such as a Nautilus Lifeline).
Be sure to take out proper diving insurance (such as DAN) in case of a diving accident. The nearest decompression chamber is hundreds of kilometers away.
There's no phone signal on board and satellite internet is limited, so share your itinerary with family in advance.
If you're prone to seasickness, take motion sickness medication before the first crossing. The overnight leg across open water is the roughest part of the trip.
Most payments on board are in cash (dollars or pesos), as card payment is limited, so bring cash for tips and extra costs.
Bring plenty of underwater camera batteries and memory, and check the onboard charging outlet type (usually 220V).
Fishing, collecting coral or shells, touching marine life, and feeding animals are all banned throughout the park, and violations carry heavy fines.
Currents are strong and can change direction suddenly at many sites, so follow your guide's instructions and never separate from your buddy.
Do not fly for at least
18–24 hours
after your last dive. It's safest to avoid an evening flight on the day you disembark.
Bad weather can change the itinerary or cancel some dive sites, and refunds may be limited in that case, so check the booking terms.
Single-use plastics are banned inside the park, and flying a drone requires a separate permit from the Tubbataha Management Office (TMO).
Tubbataha is a remote stretch of sea where emergency evacuation is very difficult. On a day when you're not feeling well, skipping the dive is the best safety rule.
